summary: Panel-mount dissolved oxygen transmitter reading 0–19.99 mg/L or 0–199.9 %, with automatic temperature compensation, isolated 4–20 mA output and dual relay control. 96 × 96 mm DIN case, 230 V AC supply.

Polarographic dissolved oxygen electrode that withstands 130 °C steam sterilisation, with a self-pressure-balancing design and an imported BJC membrane. 0.01–20 ppm range, 10 s response, 12 mm insertion diameter in 120, 280 or 450 mm lengths.
pH and ORP controller accepting a range of analogue electrodes through a built-in A/D stage. −2 to 16 pH, −2000 to 2000 mV, ±1 % FS, two 4–20 mA outputs, five relays, Modbus RTU, ABS housing, IP65.
Rod-type linear position transducer for direct coupling to a moving member. Strokes 50–1250 mm, 0.05 % linearity, 0.01 mm resolution, 100-million-cycle life, 4–20 mA or 0–10 V output, IP65.
Draw-wire position transducer measuring up to 20 m from a compact housing where a rod will not fit. 0.05 % FS repeatability, 0.25 % FS linearity, 4–20 mA or 0–10 V, stainless 316L cable, IP65.
Non-contact magnetostrictive position transducer with 0.005 % FS non-linearity and 0.002 % FS repeatability. Strokes 50–5000 mm, 4–20 mA, 0–10 V or RS485, explosion-proof, IP67. No wiper to wear out.

Linear displacement sensor with 50–1000 mm travel, 1 ms update time on four-wire connection, 0.05 % FS non-linearity and ±0.1 mm resolution. 4–20 mA or 0–10 V, aluminium housing, 304L rod, M12 five-pin connector.
Non-contact magnetostrictive position sensor, 25–2500 mm stroke, 16-bit D/A giving ±0.01 mm resolution on the voltage output. 1 ms update to 1 m stroke, 0.05 % FS non-linearity, IP67, −40 to +75 °C.

Thermal-dispersion flow switch with a single adjustable set-point, sealed all-in-one stainless body rated IP67 and 100 bar. Relay, PNP, NPN or 4–20 mA output, G1/2 thread as standard. No paddle and no moving part in the flow path, so scale and debris cannot jam it.

Two independently adjustable set-points on one thermal flow switch, giving alarm and trip from a single instrument. Two potentiometers set the thresholds; red, yellow and green LEDs report which band the flow is in. IP68 sealed body, relay or PNP/NPN output, rated to 100 bar.

Thermal flow switch with a four-digit LED display showing live flow velocity, set by two front-panel keys rather than a screwdriver. Reverse-polarity, short-circuit and overload protected. Handles media up to 100 °C and pressures to 100 bar, sealed to IP67.

Closed-loop gas flow controller combining a thermal flow sensor and a normally-closed solenoid valve in one body. Three ranges — 100, 150 and 200 L/min — with ±1 % FS accuracy, 2 s response and 5–100 % control range. Swagelok or VCR fittings, ±15 V DC supply.

Helmet-mounted TDLAS methane detector with a 60 m detection distance and 0.06 s response, so a walking inspector sweeps an area without stopping. 0–100 000 ppm·m range, 6.5 h battery, IP68, Exib IIC T4 Gb, 260 g.

Handheld TDLAS methane detector with a 100 m detection distance and 0.1 s response. 0–100 000 ppm·m, 10 h battery, IP68, Exib IIC T4, 1.2 kg. For inspecting structures that cannot be approached on foot.
Fixed explosion-proof pan-tilt head combining a TDLAS methane detector with a 40× optical zoom camera. 400–55 000 ppm·m, 100 m range, 360° continuous pan, 255 presets, 200 m IR, Exd IIC T6 Gb, IP68.

Battery-powered pressure sensor for unmanned pipeline and network monitoring. Wired, battery or cyclic supply; RS485 Modbus, I²C or 0.25–2.5 V output locally; 4G, LoRa or NB-IoT to the cloud. CE (EMC) compliant with digital temperature compensation.

Battery-powered temperature sensor for remote networks, using a Pt100/Pt1000 element in a 304 or 316 stainless probe. Wired, battery or cyclic supply; RS485 Modbus or analogue locally; 4G, LoRa or NB-IoT uplink.

Battery-powered level sensor for reservoirs, tanks and networks. Hydrostatic submersible or capacitive sensing, RS485 Modbus or analogue locally, 4G / LoRa / NB-IoT uplink. For sites with no power and no cable route.

Wireless gas sensor for toxic and combustible gas monitoring in plants and buildings, with wired or battery supply and a choice of wireless uplink. Used for confined-space safety, combustion monitoring, food and beverage process control and medical diagnostics.

Edge gateway with 4G, Wi-Fi and broadband uplinks, protocol parsing and edge computing. Local configuration software reports CPU/RAM/ROM, firmware, network state; NAT and port mapping, TLS transport encryption, hardware and software watchdog.

Discrete level switch with one to four magnetic reed points on a stainless guide rod. Passive dry contacts need no power supply, and the reed elements never touch the liquid. Rod diameter 9–25 mm, pressure to 6.3 MPa, temperature to 150 °C.

The HWS20 shares the HWS10's reed-on-rod principle with a longer, heavier-duty body for deeper tanks and wider mounting spans. Same passive dry-contact output, 1–4 set-points, 6.3 MPa and 150 °C ratings.

Injection-moulded float on a flexible rubber cable, switching 15 A at 250 V AC through an SPDT contact. Suits long cable runs, multiple points on one drop, submersible pumps and media carrying granular solids. IP68, specific gravity above 0.6.

Direct-reading magnetic flip gauge for top mounting, 200–6000 mm range, 10 MPa and up to 450 °C. Red-and-white flip column needs no power; a 4–20 mA transmitter and magnetic memory switches can be added for remote indication and alarms.

Side-mounted direct-reading magnetic flip gauge, 200–6000 mm, 10 MPa, up to 450 °C. Flange or threaded connection, optional 4–20 mA output and magnetic memory switches. Explosion-proof and corrosion-resistant construction for hazardous and high-pressure service.

Continuous level transmitter using a chain of magnetic reed modules inside a stainless guide tube. Range to 3000 mm, 4–20 mA two-wire output, 5 mm resolution, 750 Ω load. Explosion-proof aluminium housing, IP67, flange or threaded mounting.

Reed-chain level transmitter with a local LCD head showing the level on the vessel. 0–3000 mm, 4–20 mA or 1–5 V output, 5 mm resolution, explosion-proof housing, IP67. Suits tanks where operators need a local readout as well as a control-room signal.

Reed-chain level transmitter with four configurable relay outputs, bright LED display and keypad-set alarm points. 0–3000 mm range, 4–20 mA or 1–5 V output, IP67. Replaces a transmitter plus separate alarm module.
Five relay outputs plus 4–20 mA or 1–5 V, keypad-configured, with dual 24 V DC / 220 V AC supply so it can be wired straight into an existing panel. LED display, IP67, range to 3000 mm.

Non-contact magnetostrictive level transmitter, 50–5000 mm, with 0.005 % FS non-linearity and 0.002 % FS repeatability — an order of magnitude better than reed-chain instruments. 4–20 mA, 0–10 V or RS485 output, explosion-proof, IP67.

Hydrostatic level transmitter for wells, reservoirs and sumps. Range 0.05–300 m, 4–20 mA two-wire, 0.1 or 0.2 accuracy class, ceramic-capacitive or piezoresistive sensor. Ventilated cable prevents condensation, IP68.
The HPS10 hydrostatic transmitter with a local display head, so the level can be read at the well head. 0.05–300 m, 4–20 mA, accuracy class 0.1 or 0.2, IP68 probe, condensation-resistant vent.

Submersible hydrostatic transmitter with a 24-bit A/D front end, LED display, four relay outputs and 4–20 mA / 0–10 V / 1–5 V analogue output. Range 0.5–300 m, alarm points set from the keypad, stainless and aluminium housing.

Five relay outputs plus RS485 Modbus and selectable analogue output, in the 100 mm round case. 0.5–300 m range, dual 24 V DC / 110–220 V AC-DC supply, high-brightness dual-row LED. For pump control with remote supervision.

Coaxial capacitive level transmitter and controller, 100–5000 mm, with 24-bit A/D, five relays, RS485 Modbus and selectable analogue output. Handles viscous and coating media where float instruments would seize. 316 stainless probe.

Coaxial capacitive level controller with two relay outputs, LED display and 24-bit A/D. 100–5000 mm, 4–20 mA / 0–10 V / 1–5 V selectable, stainless probe. The compact option for simple high/low control on viscous media.

Microwave resonance switch that detects level through the vessel wall, so nothing protrudes into the process. Works on solids and liquids with dielectric constant above 1.5, ignores foam, and tolerates sticky conductive build-up. PEEK and stainless wetted parts, 115 °C standard or 150 °C with heat sink.

Integrated pneumatic control block for air dampers: two imported hand valves plus a vertical solenoid valve on one manifold, with automatic and manual modes that interlock so only one is active. 0.2–1.0 MPa air, DC 24/110/220 V or AC 110 V.

Laser displacement sensor with a 655 nm spot measuring a 50–400 mm centre distance, plus a 940 nm infrared TOF variant reaching 2.5 m or 4 m. Metal housing, LED display and keypad setup, four-digit readout. For dispensing, packaging, automotive and AGV duty.
Photoelectric incremental encoder with a Φ76 mm body, hollow shaft in Φ12, Φ20 or Φ25 mm, up to 2048 PPR. Supply 5 V DC, 5–30 V DC or 9–26 V DC, IP54 or IP65.
Strain-gauge load cell for 5–100 kN tension or compression, 0.1 % FS accuracy, 1.2–2.0 mV/V output, 150 % safe overload and 200 % ultimate. Stainless construction, IP65, 5–10 V DC excitation.
Stainless compression load cell for 100–5000 kg, 0.5 % FS accuracy, 1.0–2.0 mV/V output, 150 % safe and 200 % ultimate overload. IP65, 5–10 V DC excitation, Φ4 or Φ5 mm cable.

DIN-rail three-phase power meter with a dedicated metering chip, 0.55 accuracy class for active energy, full-parameter monitoring and RS485 for remote reading. LED pulse outputs to DIN 43864, LCD display, 35 mm rail mounting.

Differential pressure transmitter covering 0–0.2 kPa to 40 MPa with a 40:1 turndown and 0.2 accuracy class. Two-wire 4–20 mA, 750 Ω load, stainless housing, IP65. Built on a δ-cell capacitive sensor with a 0.10 mm measuring diaphragm.

Bidirectional differential pressure transmitter spanning −100 kPa to 200 kPa, in the standard 2088 housing with a liquid-crystal head. Two-wire 4–20 mA or three-wire 1–5 V, 0.2 accuracy class, stainless body, IP65.

Compact differential pressure transmitter, −100 kPa to 200 kPa, in a small stainless body for tight installation space. Two-wire 4–20 mA or three-wire 1–5 V, 0.2 accuracy class, G1/2 or M20×1.5, IP65.

Pressure transmitter with a 24-bit A/D, LED display, four relay outputs and selectable analogue output. −0.1 to 60 MPa, 0.2 accuracy class, diffusion-silicon, ceramic piezoresistive or ceramic capacitive sensor, stainless and aluminium housing.

Five relay outputs in a Φ150 mm gauge case, with dual 24 V DC / 220 V AC supply so it replaces a mechanical gauge in situ. −0.1 to 60 MPa, 0.2 accuracy class, high-brightness LED display, selectable analogue output.
The 100 mm version of the pressure controller: five relays, −0.1 to 60 MPa, 0.2 accuracy class, LED display, selectable analogue output. Fits the cut-out a 100 mm mechanical gauge leaves behind.

Bare Pt100 or Pt1000 probe in a stainless sheath with a standard terminal head. −200 to +600 °C, resistance signal straight out, probe length and diameter made to order. The element to specify when the transmitter lives in the panel, not on the pipe.

Pt100 probe with an integrated transmitter in the head, giving a two-wire 4–20 mA signal directly from the sensor. −200 to +600 °C, 0.1 or 0.2 accuracy class, epoxy-potted and intrinsically safe module, IP65.

Integrated temperature transmitter with a local display in the head, so the temperature is readable at the measurement point. −200 to +600 °C, two-wire 4–20 mA, 0.1 or 0.2 accuracy class, epoxy-potted, IP65.
Microcontroller-based temperature transmitter with a wide −200 to +600 °C span, 0.1 or 0.2 accuracy class, local display and two opto-isolated alarm outputs. 4–20 mA or 1–5 V, 750 Ω load, IP65.
Temperature transmitter and controller in the standard 2088 housing: 24-bit A/D, bright LED display, four relays and 4–20 mA / 1–5 V output. −200 to +600 °C, 0.1 or 0.2 accuracy class, IP65.

Five relay outputs plus RS485 Modbus on a Pt100/Pt1000 temperature transmitter. −200 to +600 °C, 24-bit A/D, LED display, parallel analogue output, IP65. For temperature control with supervisory reporting.

Bare transmitter module for mounting inside a connection head or on a DIN rail. Converts a Pt100/Pt1000 resistance to 4–20 mA, 0–5 V, 1–5 V or 0–10 V. 12–36 V supply, 0.1/0.2/0.5 accuracy class, epoxy-potted.

Fluorescent-decay temperature sensing on a quartz fibre, with no electrical path to the measurement point. −40 to +200 °C (to 300 °C on request), ±1 °C, 0.1 °C resolution, USART output, immune to electromagnetic fields and rated for 100 kV at the lead.

Replacement or additional fibre probe for the fluorescent system: ST connector, quartz fibre with PTFE jacket, rare-earth sensing tip, 3 mm overall diameter, rated to 200 °C. Bend radius 13.2 cm long-term, 4.4 cm short-term.

Complete multi-channel fibre-optic temperature system: 1–32 channels, −40 to +200 °C (300 °C on request), ±1 °C, ±0.1 °C resolution, RS485 Modbus RTU, 100–300 V AC supply, 2.3 mm probes rated for 100 kV.

M12 ultrasonic sensor with a 20–120 mm sensing range, 20 mm dead zone and 0.1 mm resolution. Detects clear glass, polished metal and liquid that optical sensors miss. PNP/NPN switching output, teach-in, IP67, 16 g.
The analogue-output member of the M12 family: 4–20 mA, 0–10 V, RS485 Modbus and IO-Link on one sensor, with a 20–120 mm range. Use it where you need the distance value, not just a switch.

M18 ultrasonic sensor, 30–300 mm range, 30 mm dead zone, 0.1 mm resolution, 22 ms response. PNP/NPN switching output with teach-in, IP67, 35 g. The general-purpose size for medium detection distances.
M18 ultrasonic sensor with a 50–500 mm range and 50 mm dead zone. 0.15 mm resolution, 32 ms response, PNP/NPN output, teach-in, IP67. For longer approaches through fixtures and guards.
Metre-range M18 ultrasonic sensor: 60–1000 mm, 60 mm dead zone, 0.17 mm resolution, 52 ms response. PNP/NPN switching, teach-in, IP67, 38 g.
Two-metre range in an M30 barrel with a 100 mm dead zone. 0.17 mm resolution, 82 ms response, PNP/NPN output, teach-in, IP67, 105 g. For warehouse and vehicle-scale distances.
Four-metre ultrasonic range in an M30 barrel: 200–4000 mm, 200 mm dead zone, 0.17–1.5 mm resolution, 162 ms response, PNP/NPN switching. For silos, large vessels and AGV obstacle detection.
intro: The DOG200 drives a polarographic dissolved oxygen electrode and displays the result in mg/L or percent saturation. It handles the compensation aeration processes actually need: temperature compensation from 0 to 65 °C, and an isolated 4–20 mA output so the signal reaching the PLC does not carry the plant's earth noise. Two relays with adjustable set-points can run a blower or an alarm directly. The 96 × 96 mm cut-out is the standard panel instrument size, which means it drops into an existing cut-out.

The DOG-208FA is built for bioreactors and fermenters, where the electrode has to survive repeated steam-in-place cycles and still hold calibration. The pressure-balancing construction prevents the membrane from being pushed off its seat when the vessel is pressurised, which is the usual failure mode for an ordinary electrode in a fermenter. The membrane head is an imported BJC type, and the body is stainless with a built-in NTC thermistor for temperature compensation, so the transmitter does not need a separate probe in the same vessel.

The PHG-2091Pro is a pH/ORP transmitter and controller that does not lock you into one electrode. A built-in A/D stage accepts the high-impedance analogue output of most pH and ORP probes, so the instrument can be brought into service with the electrode already on the vessel. Two isolated 4–20 mA outputs carry pH and temperature separately, five relays handle dosing and alarms, and Modbus RTU over RS485 reports everything to a supervisory system. The paired electrodes use a solid-electrolyte reference with a large-area PTFE junction, which resists the blocking that stops conventional references in dirty or high-solids service.

The MPS10 links a moving member to a resistive element through a rod, so the wiper position tracks the stroke directly. Linearity is 0.05 % and resolution 0.01 mm, which is enough for press depth, gate position and valve travel. The 100-million-cycle life comes from the contact design and the special laser trimming of the track; where the duty will exceed that, the non-contact MMS10 is the instrument to specify. Travel speed is up to 5 m/s in the standard version and 10 m/s in the high-speed version.

A draw-wire transducer unreels a stainless cable from a spring-loaded drum and measures the rotation. Because the cable is flexible, the measuring range can be long while the body stays small — up to 20 m from a unit that fits in your hand. That makes it the practical choice for overhead cranes, telescopic booms, lift travel and anything where a 10 m rod is not an option. Linearity is 0.25 % FS and repeatability 0.05 % FS, so it is a positioning instrument rather than a metrology reference.

The MMS10 times a torsional pulse along a waveguide to a permanent magnet on the moving member. Nothing touches the sensing element, so there is no wiper to wear, no contact resistance to drift and no limit on the number of cycles — the reason magnetostrictive is used for injection-moulding clamps, servo-hydraulic actuators and any duty where a contact transducer would be replaced regularly. Non-linearity is 0.005 % FS and repeatability 0.002 % FS, roughly an order of magnitude better than a resistive rod.

The ER series is a shorter-stroke, faster-updating position sensor for general automation. Update time is 1 ms on the four-wire connection, which is quick enough to close a position loop rather than merely report a position. Resolution is ±0.1 mm below 400 mm of travel and range/4096 above it. The aluminium extrusion carries a 304L stainless rod and terminates in an M12 five-pin aviation connector, so it drops into a standard machine wiring harness.

The ESC is a compact non-contact sensor for strokes up to 2.5 m, with a 16-bit D/A converter that gives ±0.01 mm resolution on the voltage output. Because the magnet slides without touching the waveguide, there is no wear limit and no restriction on magnet speed. Update time scales with stroke — 1 ms up to 1 m, 2 ms to 2 m, 3 ms beyond — which is worth knowing when the stroke is long and the loop is fast. The PFA rod and PP head suit washdown and mildly aggressive environments.

The HSM10 detects flow by heating a probe slightly above the medium temperature and measuring how quickly that heat is carried away. Moving liquid or gas removes heat faster than a still column, so the electronics can decide whether the pipe is flowing and trip a relay at your set-point. Because the sensing element is a solid stainless probe with no paddle, vane or orifice, there is nothing for scale, sludge or debris to block. The probe face receives a surface treatment that resists the corrosion and fouling that shorten the life of ordinary flow switches in poor-quality water. Once the trip point is set, the unit holds it without periodic adjustment, which matters on plant that cannot tolerate an instrument drifting out of calibration.

The HSM20 is the HSM10 with two set-points instead of one. Two potentiometers are adjusted independently, so you can set a low threshold that raises a warning and a second threshold that trips the plant, from the same probe. Three indicator states — red below the first set-point, yellow above the first, green above the second — let an operator read the flow band from across the room without a display or a control system. The all-in-one sealed construction is rated IP68 rather than IP67, so the body survives washdown and temporary flooding. It uses the same thermal-dispersion principle and the same treated 316L probe as the rest of the range, which means the same immunity to fouling and the same absence of moving parts.

The HSM30 replaces the potentiometer with a digital display and a two-key interface. Instead of guessing at a screw position, the maintenance technician reads the actual velocity on the LED display, presses the key when the flow is at the value they want, and the trip point is stored. That makes commissioning repeatable across several identical machines, and it makes fault-finding possible without a separate flow meter: if the pump is running and the display reads zero, the problem is upstream. The electronics include reverse-polarity, short-circuit and overload protection, which is the difference between a blown fuse and a dead instrument on a badly wired panel. It also extends the medium temperature ceiling to 100 °C, above the 80 °C limit of the analogue models.

Where the HSM switches detect flow, the S400 regulates it. A thermal sensor measures the actual flow and a normally-closed solenoid valve modulates in response, so the controller holds the set-point instead of merely reporting it. Control range is 5–100 % of full scale, which means the valve still has authority at low flow rather than shutting off abruptly. Linearity is ±0.5 % FS and repeatability ±0.2 % FS, with a 2 s settling time to within ±2 % of set-point. Accuracy is specified between 15 and 35 °C; outside that band the unit still works, but the specification widens. Body is rated to 3 MPa with a helium leak rate below 1×10⁻² Pa·m³/s, and the fittings are Swagelok 3/8″ or 10 mm, or VCR 1/2″.

TDLAS works by tuning a diode laser across a methane absorption line and measuring how much light is absorbed along the round trip to a surface and back. Because the measurement is path-integrated rather than point, the instrument reports the concentration along the beam — which is what you want when you are looking for a leak somewhere on a pipe rack 30 m away. Mounted on a hard hat, it frees both hands and lets the operator point the visible green aiming laser while walking. The 0.06 s response is the figure that makes walking inspection practical: the detector reacts as fast as the beam sweeps across a plume.

The handheld counterpart to the wearable unit, with double the detection distance and a battery that lasts a working shift. At 100 m the beam reaches elevated pipework, tank roofs and flare stacks that would otherwise require scaffolding or a climb. Low false-alarm rate matters more at this distance, because the operator cannot easily walk over and confirm: TDLAS is selective for methane and does not respond to other hydrocarbons, dust or water vapour the way a catalytic or infrared point sensor would.

A fixed installation version of the same TDLAS measurement, mounted on a pan-tilt head with a 40× zoom camera. The value is in the combination: the detector finds a plume, the camera zooms in on it, and the operator sees both the concentration and the physical location — a leaking flange rather than a sector of the plant. Continuous 360° pan, 255 presets and eight cruise patterns mean the unit can sweep a tank farm on a schedule, and the image is available over standard video interfaces with alarm inputs and outputs for integration.

Built for the places where there is no mains power and no cable route: oil and gas gathering lines, heating networks, fire-water mains and remote valve chambers. The sensing element is a low-power pressure die with on-chip temperature compensation, calibrated values stored in the chip and applied automatically, so winter-to-summer drift does not appear as a pressure change. Locally the sensor gives RS485 Modbus RTU, I²C or a 0.25–2.5 V analogue output; remotely it reports over 4G, LoRa or NB-IoT, and the data lands in a cloud platform for storage and trending.

A platinum element in a stainless sheath, packaged with a low-power radio and a battery. The Pt100/Pt1000 response is linear with temperature, so the calibration is stable and the reading can be checked against a reference at any time. Intended for supply networks, environmental monitoring, cold chain, HV transmission assets and any site where a walk-round temperature check is currently the only option.

Two sensing principles in one product family: a submersible hydrostatic probe that converts head pressure to level, and a capacitive probe that measures the change in capacitance as the level rises. The choice depends on the medium — hydrostatic for clean water in deep wells, capacitive for tanks where a suspended probe is impractical. Both are packaged with the same low-power radio and battery, so a site can mix the two and use one gateway.

A gas sensing element with a low-power radio, for locations where a fixed wired detector would mean a cable route across a plant. Applications range from safety monitoring for toxic and combustible gases in oil, mining and semiconductor facilities through to combustion efficiency in flues, sulphur dioxide control in food and beverage processing, and diagnostic measurement such as blood carbon dioxide and oxygen concentration.

The gateway is the piece that turns sensor traffic into usable data. It accepts 4G, Wi-Fi and broadband uplinks, parses industrial protocols, and forwards the results — either to a cloud platform or to a local SCADA — with TLS encryption on the transport. Edge computing capability means some of the processing happens before the data leaves the site, which reduces both bandwidth cost and latency. Local configuration software reports CPU utilisation, RAM and ROM usage, hostname, model, firmware and kernel version, uptime and network state, and the unit ships with a firewall supporting NAT and port mapping. A hardware and software watchdog pair keeps it running unattended.

The HWS10 places one or more magnetic reed elements inside a stainless guide rod; a float carrying a permanent magnet rides up and down the rod and closes each reed as it passes. Because the contact is passive, the switch needs no supply — two wires are enough. The reed element is sealed inside the rod, so it never sees the medium; only stainless steel does. Up to four points can be positioned anywhere along the rod to your drawing, which makes one instrument do the job of several. Simple, with no electronics to drift and nothing to calibrate.

Where the HWS10 mounts close to the vessel, the HWS20 extends the rod and terminal arrangement for tanks with thick insulation or long nozzles. The sensing principle is unchanged: a magnetic float trips sealed reed elements inside a stainless rod, producing passive dry contacts with no supply wiring. Up to four points can be set to your drawing, each with a separate pair of wires, and the wetted parts are all stainless so the switch tolerates water, oil and mildly aggressive media.

The HLS01 hangs a sealed float from a rubber cable. As the liquid rises the float tilts, a steel ball inside rolls and operates a microswitch, and the SPDT contact changes state. The 15 A rating is high enough to switch a pump directly, without a contactor, which is unusual for a float of this size. Because the float is small and the cable flexible, several can be hung at different depths on one drop to give multi-point control. It tolerates granular and lumpy media that would jam a guided float, and the cord grip and moulding are rated IP68.

A magnetic level gauge is a manometer with a magnetic twist: a float inside the chamber carries a magnet, and that magnet flips small bicolour vanes on the outside as the level moves. The boundary between red and white is the level. No power, no electronics, nothing to drift — an operator reads it through a window and trusts it. The HTS11 is the top-mounted pattern for vessels where the side is obstructed. Add the optional 4–20 mA transmitter for a control-room signal and magnetic memory switches for alarms, and the same instrument covers local and remote indication. Rated to 10 MPa and available for media up to 450 °C.

The side-mounted pattern is the standard arrangement for a vertical tank with accessible side nozzles. A float in the chamber follows the liquid, its magnet flips the external bicolour vanes, and the red/white boundary is the level. Because the chamber is sealed and the vanes are outside it, the gauge suits flammable, high-pressure and high-temperature service where a glass sight glass would be a risk. The optional transmitter gives a 4–20 mA signal, and magnetic memory switches latch at set levels so an alarm stays on after the level has passed.

Instead of separate switch points, the HWT10 fills the guide tube with a series of reed modules and precision resistors. A magnetic float closes the reeds at its own height, and the resulting resistance is converted to a continuous 4–20 mA signal proportional to level. The electronics live inside an explosion-proof aluminium housing, and the tube and float are 316L or 304 stainless, so the instrument suits fuel and chemical tanks as well as water. There is no capacitive drift and no ultrasonic dead zone; the output follows the float directly.

The HWT20 is the HWT10 with an LCD head. The measuring element is the same reed-and-resistor chain, so the output follows the float with no drift and no dead zone, but the technician standing at the tank can read the level directly instead of trusting that the signal is right. Output is 4–20 mA or 1–5 V, both with 750 Ω load capability, and the aluminium housing is explosion-proof for flammable service.

The HWT2088 adds a controller to the reed-chain transmitter: four relays, each with an alarm point set from the front keypad, alongside the standard analogue output. That means a single instrument can start and stop a pump, raise high and low alarms, and still feed a 4–20 mA signal to the control room, without a separate trip amplifier. The LED display is readable in daylight, and the settings are changed by key rather than by internal jumpers, so a change of duty does not need the housing opened.

The HWT100 is the top of the magnetic-induction range: five relays instead of four, and a supply that accepts either 24 V DC or 220 V AC. That dual supply matters in retrofit work, where the panel may only have a 220 V rail available and adding a 24 V power supply is an extra component and an extra failure point. Everything else follows the family: reed-chain measurement, LED display, keypad-set points, and a parallel analogue output.

Magnetostrictive measurement sends a current pulse down a waveguide and times the return twist produced where the float's magnet sits. There is no contact between the float and the sensing element, so nothing wears and accuracy does not degrade with use — non-linearity is 0.005 % FS and repeatability 0.002 % FS, which is roughly ten times better than a reed chain. Because the waveguide reports position and velocity, the same instrument can serve custody-transfer-adjacent duties and interface measurement in a tank with two liquids. Explosion-proof construction and a 316 stainless rod make it suitable for fuel and chemical service.

The HPS10 measures hydrostatic head: the pressure at the bottom of a column of liquid is proportional to its height, so a pressure sensor lowered to the bottom of a well reads the level directly once you enter the density. The ceramic-capacitive element is temperature-compensated and linearised before the 4–20 mA conversion, and the accuracy class is 0.1 or 0.2. A ventilated cable equalises the reference side with atmosphere so barometric changes do not appear as level changes, and the vent design resists condensation, which is the usual failure mode for submersible transmitters in cool wells.

Same hydrostatic sensing element as the HPS10, with a display in the head so the reading is visible where the cable is terminated. In practice that saves the maintenance technician from carrying a multimeter to every well to check whether the transmitter is alive, and it makes hydrostatic readings comparable with a manual dip without opening the control cabinet.

The HPS2088 puts the measurement and the control in the same head: a hydrostatic probe feeds a 24-bit A/D converter, the microcontroller linearises and displays the depth, and four relays act on your alarm points. For a pump station that otherwise needs a transmitter plus a separate level relay, that is one instrument instead of two, and one calibration instead of two that can disagree. Analogue output is selectable between 4–20 mA, 0–10 mA, 0–10 V and 0–5 V.

The HPS100 is the communications-equipped member of the family: five relays, RS485 Modbus for supervisory systems, and a 24 V DC or 110–220 V AC-DC supply so it can be dropped into an existing panel. The 100 mm round case takes the place of a standard pressure gauge, which makes it a straightforward retrofit where a mechanical gauge currently sits and someone has to walk out and read it. Dual-row LED display shows live value and set-points at the same time.

Capacitance measurement uses the medium itself as the dielectric between two coaxial electrodes. As the level rises, more of the probe is immersed, the capacitance changes, and the electronics convert that to a level. There is no float to jam and nothing that needs to move, which is why capacitive instruments are used on slurries, viscous products and media that coat — the three cases where a float switch stops working. The 24-bit front end resolves the small capacitance change, and five relays plus RS485 cover both local control and supervisory reporting.

A two-relay version of the capacitive controller for duties that only need high and low: fill-and-drain on a small tank, high-level alarm plus low-level cut-out on a day tank. The measuring element is identical to the HCT100, so the same suitability for viscous and coating media applies, and the plastic or aluminium housing is lighter where the instrument is bracket-mounted rather than panel-mounted.

The VB106/107 forms a high-frequency resonant circuit between its probe, its metal housing and the internal electronics. When medium covers the probe — or when the local dielectric constant changes — the resonant frequency shifts, and the unit compares the new frequency against your alarm setting. The consequence is a switch that does not care about foam, does not care about sticky or conductive build-up on the probe, and works on solids as well as liquids. Because it can be mounted to sense through the wall, it also serves hygienic vessels where a protruding probe would create a cleaning problem. PEEK and stainless are the wetted materials, so it holds up in food, pharmaceutical and industrial service.

A damper on a duct needs more than one actuator: it needs to open, close, and reverse-flush, under either automatic or manual control. The SBG10 puts all of that on one aluminium manifold — two imported hand valves and a vertical solenoid valve, with the mode selected by turning the left-hand valve. In automatic, the right-hand valve sits at zero and the solenoid's left and right coils drive close and reverse-flush. Switch to manual, and the right-hand valve selects close or flush directly. The two modes interlock mechanically, so an operator cannot be fighting the solenoid. A pressure gauge module and filter can be added on the same block.

Two measurement techniques in one family. The 655 nm triangulation sensor measures 50 mm to 400 mm from the housing face with a small, bright spot — the right tool for gap, step and height on a dispenser, a filling nozzle or a packaging web. The 940 nm time-of-flight variant measures 2.5 m or 4 m and carries a visible aiming beam, which suits AGV obstacle sensing and vehicle positioning over a long range. Both share a metal housing, a four-digit white LED display and keypad configuration, so switching between the versions on one machine does not change the setup procedure.

An incremental encoder turns shaft rotation into a pulse train, and the control system counts pulses to derive speed and position. The photoelectric sensing principle gives clean edges at high resolution; 2048 pulses per revolution on a Φ76 mm body suits most general machine-feedback duties. The hollow-shaft mounting slides directly over the machine shaft, which avoids the coupling alignment problems that shorten the life of a solid-shaft encoder.

A strain-gauge bridge bonded to a machined element: force deflects the element, the gauges change resistance, and the bridge outputs a millivolt signal proportional to load. The 0.1 % FS accuracy class and 1.2–2.0 mV/V sensitivity are the standard figures a weighing or force-control amplifier expects, so the cell drops into existing instrumentation without a special interface. Temperature compensation is applied over −10 to +40 °C, with sensitivity and zero drift both held to ±0.1 % FS per 10 °C.

A weighing cell rather than a force-measurement cell: 100 kg to 5 tonnes, 0.5 % FS, stainless body, sealed to IP65. The 0.5 % class is the appropriate grade for tank weighing, hopper content and platform scales, where the accuracy requirement is content estimation rather than force calibration. Both sensitivity and zero are compensated across −10 to +40 °C.

A dedicated metering chip measures three-phase voltage, current, power, power factor, frequency and imported/exported energy at 0.55 accuracy class, and the LCD shows any of them. RS485 Modbus allows remote meter reading, so a sub-distribution board can be monitored without hiring an energy contractor. The pulse outputs for active and reactive energy follow DIN 43864, which means an existing pulse-counting system can be connected without changes, and the 35 mm rail mount fits standard enclosures.

The PDD3051 uses a δ-cell: a tensioned measuring diaphragm between two capacitor plates, with the process pressure transmitted to it through fill fluid and isolating diaphragms on the high and low sides. Diaphragm displacement is at most 0.10 mm, and the change in capacitance is converted linearly to a two-wire 4–20 mA signal. The practical benefit of the 40:1 turndown is that one transmitter model covers a wide span, so a plant can standardise on a single spare instead of stocking a range for every application. Non-linearity is 0.2, hysteresis is under 0.01 % of span, and long-term stability is 0.15 % FS per year.

The PDD2088 covers the low-pressure end where most differential measurements actually live: draught, filter loading, cleanroom and duct pressure, and low-range level. It reads both directions, from −100 kPa to +200 kPa, so gauge and vacuum duties share one model. Output is two-wire 4–20 mA or three-wire 1–5 V, and the 2088 housing is the industry-standard shape, which means existing brackets, manifolds and spare parts fit. Process connection is G1/2 or M20×1.5, with custom threads available.

The PDD1020 does the same job as the PDD2088 in a smaller stainless housing, for panels and skids where the 2088 head will not fit or where the extra volume is simply not needed. The measuring range and accuracy are identical, as are the electrical options, so a plant can mix the two without introducing a second set of spares, wiring conventions or configuration instructions.

The PCD2088 pairs a pressure sensor with a controller in one 2088 head: 24-bit conversion, a display readable across a plant room, four relays with keypad-set trip points, and a selectable analogue output to the control system. It is the right instrument when a pressure switch and a transmitter are both currently installed on the same line — one device then covers measurement, local indication and interlock, and there is only one calibration record to keep. Sensor type is selected to suit the medium: diffusion silicon for clean gas and liquid, ceramic piezoresistive or capacitive for chemically aggressive service.

The PCC216 is built into a 150 mm round case — the size of a standard process pressure gauge — so it drops into an existing gauge mounting without a bracket or a panel cut-out. Five relays, a dual 24 V DC / 220 V AC supply and a bright LED display make it a direct functional replacement for a gauge that someone currently has to walk out and read, with alarm and interlock capability added at the same time. The 216 designation refers to the case size, not to a 216 mm dimension.

Where space is tighter, the PCC100 provides the same five-relay control in a 100 mm case. It is the instrument to specify when a 150 mm gauge will not fit but the duty still calls for local display, alarms and an analogue signal to the control room. Storage temperature extends to 120 °C, useful in hot valve rooms.

The TPS10 is the sensing element on its own: a high-accuracy platinum resistance element in a stainless tube, with the internals packed in a thermally conductive compound so the element follows the process temperature rather than lagging behind it. The resistance follows the standard Pt100 index table exactly, which means the reading is interchangeable with any other compliant instrument and can be verified with a decade box at commissioning. Where a 4–20 mA output is wanted, the TPT family adds a transmitter module to the same probe.

The TPT10 puts the transmitter on the probe rather than in the panel. The element's resistance is linearised, protected against supply reversal, and converted to a two-wire 4–20 mA current in the head, so the cable run carries a signal that does not pick up resistance error from long leads. The module is epoxy-potted, which is what makes it survive vibration and humidity in a plant room, and it is an intrinsically safe design for hazardous areas. Accuracy class is 0.1 or 0.2, and the probe length is made to your requirement.

The TPT20 is the TPT10 with a display head. On plant where the maintenance team walks the line, that removes the need to interrogate the control system to see whether a sensor has failed — they can look at it. The electrical and mechanical specification is otherwise the same, so the two models are interchangeable in a spares strategy.

The TPT201 replaces the analogue transmitter circuit with an industrial microcontroller and a high-resolution A/D converter. The practical difference is range flexibility: one model spans from −200 to +600 °C without a range card, and the same unit can be configured for a narrow band where a finer resolution is needed. Two opto-isolated alarm outputs are available (not fitted as standard) for high and low temperature trips, and the local display shows the process value.

The TPT2088 is the temperature member of the 2088 controller family. It reads a Pt100 or Pt1000 element through a 24-bit converter, displays the value on a high-brightness LED, and operates four relays against keypad-set set-points, while providing an analogue output in parallel. On a heater bank or a heat-treatment furnace it replaces the transmitter plus a separate temperature trip, and the set-points can be adjusted from the front without opening the housing.

The TPT100 adds RS485 Modbus and a fifth relay to the temperature controller. The communications port is what makes it useful on a plant with a supervisory system: the same instrument that runs the local interlock can report the measured value and the relay states to a SCADA or building-management system, so the operator does not have to infer what happened from a separate data logger.

The TPT00 is the electronics without the probe. It is what you fit when the sensor already exists — when a probe is being replaced, or when a panel needs to condition several RTD inputs in one enclosure. Because it is epoxy-potted, it can go inside a field connection head where condensation is likely, and the four selectable output types cover most legacy control-system inputs without needing signal converters.

A fluorescent material at the fibre tip is excited by a light pulse; how quickly its glow decays depends on temperature, and the decay is timed optically. There is no electrical connection between the sensing tip and the instrument — no thermocouple, no RTD lead, no metal path. That is the whole point: at 100 kV, a metal probe in a transformer winding is a liability, while a quartz fibre is not. The same property makes the sensor immune to electromagnetic interference, immune to chemical attack, and small enough to place in a winding hot spot or a switchgear contact.

The probe is the consumable part of a fibre-optic temperature system. It carries light from the module to the sensing tip and back, and it is the part exposed to the process. The quartz core is clad and then sheathed in PTFE, so the fibre survives chemicals that would attack a plastic-jacketed cable, and the ST connector is a standard fit for the transmitter module. Probes are supplied in standard 5 m lengths and can be ordered shorter or longer.

The system pairs a multi-channel transmitter with a set of fluorescent probes. Each channel is independent and interrogated in turn, so one instrument covers every hot spot in a transformer, a switchgear line-up or a cable trench. Output is RS485 Modbus RTU, which means the values land directly in a SCADA or protection relay without an intermediate converter. Because the probes contain no metal and carry no current, the installation does not compromise the insulation coordination of the equipment being monitored — which is the reason this technique exists at all.

A 120 mm ultrasonic sensor in an M12 barrel for close-range presence detection where optical sensing is unreliable. Sound reflects from any surface with an acoustic impedance mismatch, so clear PET bottles, mirror-finish stainless and dark matte rubber all return an echo — the three cases where a photoelectric sensor gives up. The 20 mm dead zone means the target can be brought quite close to the face, and 0.1 mm resolution allows more than just presence detection: the analogue-window behaviour is good enough for simple positioning.

Same acoustic front end as the UB120, with an output stage that reports the measured distance rather than a threshold crossing. Four interfaces are available on the same body — 4–20 mA, 0–10 V, RS485 Modbus RTU and IO-Link — so the sensor can be specified once and integrated into whichever control platform the machine uses. That matters for machine builders who ship the same mechanism to customers with different PLC standards.

The 300 mm range in an M18 barrel is the workhorse of the family — long enough to clear fixtures and guarding, short enough to keep the sound cone tight. At 22 ms response and 45 Hz switching frequency it handles conveyor speeds without missing items, and the ±2 mm hysteresis stops chatter on a target that sits near the threshold.

Half a metre of range from the same M18 barrel, for applications where the sensor has to sit behind a guard or outside a spray zone and still see the target. Resolution drops slightly to 0.15 mm and response extends to 32 ms, which is still fast enough for most packaging and materials-handling duties.

One metre of range in an 18 mm barrel is useful for bin and hopper work where the sensor mounts on the lid and has to see the product surface at low fill. Sound at these distances spreads widely, so mount away from side walls and structural steel — the 60 mm dead zone is the near limit, but the practical limit is usually reflection from surrounding surfaces.

The M30 barrel carries a larger transducer, which is what makes 2 m possible. Response extends to 82 ms — still adequate for a vehicle entering a bay or a stacker approaching a rack, but not for fast small-item counting. The 100 mm dead zone should be kept clear of fixtures.

The longest range in the family, and the one where mounting discipline matters most. At 4 m the sound cone is wide and the return is weak, so the target needs a reasonable surface area and the background needs to be either far enough away or handled by the sensor's window setting. Response is 162 ms, appropriate for slowly changing distances rather than fast scanning.
